questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: A forklift turns quickly with an elevated off-center load. Why does tip-over risk increase?
options: The engine torque automatically doubles the rated capacity
The combined center of gravity can move outside the stability triangle
The rear wheels permanently lock during every turn
Raising the load lowers the combined center of gravity
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Turning, elevation, and off-center loading shift the combined center of gravity toward or beyond the stability boundary.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Engine torque does not increase rated capacity and does not explain lateral instability.
Rear-wheel steering changes handling, but the wheels do not automatically lock.
Raising the load raises the center of gravity and generally reduces stability.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, powered industrial trucks and workplace conditions, pp. 702-712

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: A forklift is rated for 4,000 pounds at a 24-inch load center. Ignoring other limits, what approximate load produces the same load moment at a 30-inch center?
options: 2,400 pounds
4,000 pounds
3,200 pounds
5,000 pounds
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Maintain the same moment: 4,000*24 = W*30, so W = 3,200 pounds.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This applies the ratio in the wrong direction and reduces capacity too far.
Rated capacity at 24 inches cannot simply be used at the longer load center.
A longer load center reduces, rather than increases, the equivalent allowable load.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, powered industrial truck load and stability principles, pp. 702-712
questions.formula: rated load*rated center = allowable load*actual center

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: An operator finds a hydraulic leak during the pre-use inspection. What is the correct response?
options: Operate it only with a lighter load
Wipe the leak and continue until the shift ends
Use it outdoors because ventilation is better
Remove the truck from service until the unsafe condition is corrected
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Powered industrial trucks should not be placed in service when inspection identifies a condition that adversely affects safe operation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Reducing the load does not eliminate loss of hydraulic function or fire and slip hazards.
Cleaning evidence of the leak does not correct the defect.
Outdoor use does not address the unsafe mechanical condition.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, powered industrial trucks, pp. 702-712; OSHA 1910.178

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: How often must each powered-industrial-truck operator performance be evaluated at a minimum?
options: At least once every three years
Every month
Only at initial assignment
Every five years
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA requires an evaluation of each operator performance at least once every three years, with refresher training when specified conditions occur.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Monthly evaluation is not the minimum interval stated by the standard.
Initial training alone is insufficient; periodic evaluation is required.
Five years exceeds the specified minimum evaluation interval.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, powered industrial truck training, pp. 702-710; OSHA 1910.178(l)

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: Before a forklift enters a trailer across a portable dockboard, which verification is most important?
options: The forklift horn is loud enough
The dockboard is secured and rated, and the trailer is restrained against movement
The trailer doors are fully open
The driver remains seated in the tractor
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Safe dock transfer depends on adequate dockboard capacity and securement plus prevention of trailer movement.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A horn does not control dockboard displacement or trailer separation.
Open doors provide access but do not establish capacity or restraint.
Driver presence does not reliably prevent trailer movement and may create communication uncertainty.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, loading docks and entering semi-trailers, pp. 710-712; OSHA material handling

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: Palletized materials are leaning into an aisle after partial removal. What is the best response?
options: Mark the pallet with caution tape and continue work
Rely on workers to walk on the opposite side of the aisle
Restack or secure the material before allowing continued access
Increase the stack height to improve compression
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Stored materials must remain stable and secure against sliding or collapse, with aisles kept safely clear.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Tape communicates the hazard but does not stabilize the load.
Avoidance depends on behavior and leaves the unstable stack in service.
Increasing height raises potential energy and is likely to reduce stability.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, materials storage and storage racks, pp. 687-715; OSHA 1910.176

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: A symmetric two-leg sling supports a 2,000-pound load. Each leg is 60 degrees above horizontal. Ignoring sling weight, what is the approximate tension in each leg?
options: 577 pounds
1,000 pounds
1,732 pounds
1,155 pounds
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For two equal legs, 2*T*sin(60)=2,000. T=2,000/(2*0.866)=approximately 1,155 pounds.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides by an extra factor of two after resolving the vertical components.
This assumes each leg carries half the load without accounting for sling angle.
This multiplies the half-load by the sine relationship rather than dividing by it.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, materials handling and rigging principles, pp. 687-715; ASP11 rigging calculations

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: A dense component has no good handholds and must be moved repeatedly. Which control should be considered first?
options: Use a mechanical assist or redesign the component and handling method
Teach workers to lift faster
Require back belts as the primary control
Use only a team-lift label without evaluating the load
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Mechanical assistance or redesign reduces the load and exposure at the source, which is stronger than behavior-dependent methods.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Speed can increase loss of control and does not reduce the physical load.
Back belts do not substitute for reducing force, reach, and handling demand.
A label does not establish that a team lift is feasible or adequately controlled.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapters 24 and 30, manual material handling and lifting techniques, pp. 546-566 and 687-695

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: A jammed conveyor must be cleared inside a guarded area. What is the strongest required approach?
options: Use the emergency stop as the only isolation
Stop and isolate hazardous energy, verify isolation, and control stored or potential energy before entry
Have a spotter watch the start button
Clear the jam while the conveyor runs at reduced speed
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Servicing that exposes workers to unexpected startup or stored energy requires an energy-control procedure and verification.
incorrectOptionExplanations: An emergency stop is a control device and may not physically isolate energy.
A spotter does not prevent unexpected energization or stored-energy release.
Reduced speed still exposes the worker to moving and stored energy.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapters 4 and 30, hazardous energy control and conveyors, pp. 68-71 and 713-715; OSHA 1910.147

questions.chapterTitle: Materials Handling, Powered Industrial Trucks, and Rigging
questions.stem: A crane is positioning a load while another crew plans to walk under it to save time. What is the best decision?
options: Allow crossing if hard hats are worn
Allow one person at a time to pass quickly
Stop the crossing and maintain an exclusion zone beneath the suspended load
Permit crossing when the operator sounds the horn
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Employees should be kept clear of suspended loads and the fall zone because rigging or equipment failure can be catastrophic.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Hard hats cannot protect against the energy of a falling suspended load.
Short exposure time does not make the consequence acceptable.
A warning signal does not prevent a dropped or shifting load.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 30, materials handling and lifting equipment, pp. 687-715
